world.title: MALAWI: Catholic Sisters Challenged to Make Social Entrepreneurship a Force for Human Development
world.desc:
By Brenard Mwanza
The Auxiliary Bishop of the Archdiocese of Lilongwe, Right Reverend Vincent Frederick Mwakhwawa, has challenged Catholic Sisters in Malawi to use social entrepreneurship as a tool for advancing the Church’s mission, promoting human dignity and contributing to human development in their communities.
Bishop Mwakhwawa made the call on Friday, 7 August 2026, during the graduation ceremony of the Sisters’ Blended Value Project Social Entrepreneurship Programme in Lilongwe, held under the theme, “Faith in Action: Women Religious Leading Sustainable and Scalable Social Enterprises.”
Representing Bishop Peter Adrian Chifukwa, President of the Association of Women Religious Institutes of Malawi (AWRIM) and the Association of Men Religious Institutes of Malawi (AMRIM) at the Malawi Conference of Catholic Bishops (MCCB), Bishop Mwakhwawa said the entrepreneurial skills acquired through the programme should serve a purpose beyond financial sustainability.
“The entrepreneurial skills you have acquired are not merely for financial sustainability; they are instruments for advancing the missionary works of the Church, for evangelisation, preaching the Gospel, bringing Christ to others, building the Kingdom of God, restoring human dignity, creating opportunities for others and strengthening the ministries entrusted to your congregations,” he said.
He described the graduation as “the beginning of a renewed mission”, and encouraged the sisters to place the needs of people at the centre of their enterprises.
Reflecting on the theme, Bishop Mwakhwawa placed particular emphasis on the word “scalable”, challenging the graduates to develop initiatives whose impact can extend beyond their immediate communities.
“We should not be satisfied only when one enterprise succeeds in one community. We should ask whether successful ideas can be adapted, replicated and expanded so that their benefits reach many more people,” he said.
He urged the graduates to build their enterprises around five principles: responding to genuine community needs; managing them professionally and transparently; measuring social impact alongside financial performance; working collaboratively; and remaining open to learning, adaptation and innovation.
Drawing on Catholic Social Teaching, Bishop Mwakhwawa said social entrepreneurship can contribute to integral human development when guided by Gospel values.
He cited Pope St Paul VI’s 1967 Encyclical Populorum Progressio, which emphasises that authentic development must place the human person at the centre rather than focus solely on the accumulation of wealth.
The Bishop also called for continued mentorship and follow-up as the graduates begin applying their newly acquired skills in their communities.
He described the certificates presented to the Sisters as not only recognition of their achievement, but also a responsibility to place their knowledge and skills at the service of God’s people.
“May the enterprises you establish not only generate resources but also transform lives, empower young people, support vulnerable families, and contribute to the holistic development of our nation,” he said.
The Sisters’ Blended Value Project seeks to strengthen the capacity of Catholic Sisters to establish sustainable social enterprises through skills development, networking, information hubs, and access to financial services.
Funded by the Conrad N. Hilton Foundation, the initiative is implemented by Strathmore University Business School in Kenya in partnership with the Association of Consecrated Women in Eastern and Central Africa (ACWECA).
The project is being implemented in Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, Tanzania and Malawi, to equip women religious with the skills, networks and support needed to establish and sustain social enterprises beyond the grant period.
Bishop Mwakhwawa commended ACWECA for its vision and commitment to empowering women religious and recognised AWRIM for coordinating the initiative in Malawi.
The programme highlights the growing role of women religious in using innovative and sustainable approaches to strengthen the Church’s social mission and contribute to the integral development of communities across the region.

world.title: SIGNIS: Organizers of 2027 World Youth Day Build Integrated Media Ecosystem
world.desc:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
The Organizers of the 2027 World Youth Day (WYD) in Seoul have unveiled plans for an integrated media ecosystem to bring the pilgrimage to young people around the globe, whether or not they can travel to South Korea for the event.
Speaking about the media network at the SIGNIS World Congress in Rwanda, Fr. Dominic Jaehyu Lee, the Deputy Director of the Communications Division of the local organizing committee for WYD Seoul 2027, told delegates that while the pilgrimage to Seoul is already underway, organizers are focused on a broader concern on how to remain visible, connected, and accessible even to those who will not be physically present in Seoul.
To meet that challenge, the Communications Division has structured its media framework for the 2027 event around four connected pillars: The press center, which will support journalists and production teams covering the event on site; the host broadcaster, which will provide the technical foundation and produce the international signal for worldwide distribution, the WYD Now, which will provide official digital live programming and global distribution and the Catholic Peace Broadcasting Company, (CPBC) the official Catholic broadcaster, which will foster collaboration among Catholic media outlets and also serve as a bridge between faith and communication.
Fr. Lee emphasized that although each pillar carries a distinct responsibility, none stands alone. WYD Now, jointly developed by the Communications Division and CPBC, sits at the center of this system, tasked with connecting official live signals, programming from different venues, partner content, and Catholic media from around the world.
Unlike a conventional broadcast channel, WYD Now is being built as an official digital media collaboration network rather than simply another streaming outlet. Through it, Catholic media organizations will be able to access reliable, official WYD Seoul 2027 content adapted to their own languages and local contexts, while also sending stories from their own young people back to Seoul.
WYD Now is not designed as a system in which Seoul produces, and the rest of the world simply receives, Fr. Lee said, and emphasized that it is a two-way structure through which Seoul and local churches can exchange stories, images, prayer, and witness.
Participation will vary according to each organization's capacity, he explained. A broadcaster might carry the official live feed with commentary or subtitles in its own language; a news outlet or digital platform might use approved clips and photos for reporting and social media; a media organization on site might contribute its own signal or content for global sharing; and local churches might send testimonies, prayers, and stories from their own communities.
Registration and cooperation, Fr. Lee noted, do not begin when the main events open in August 2027, but they begin now, at the SIGNIS Congress itself.
Media organizations that register with WYD Now will receive information in stages: first, key dates, preparation updates, and downloadable official materials such as logos, photographs, and promotional videos; later, broadcast planning details, technical specifications, guidance on official video and live-feed usage, subtitle and language resources, and schedule updates.
Organizers also plan to establish an ongoing point of contact so that questions from partner media can be received and directed to the right person within the organizing committee. Access to information matters, but access to a trusted relationship matters even more, Fr. Lee said.
During the main event, WYD Now will consolidate coverage of major celebrations with the Holy Father, the Youth Festival, catechesis, prayer, and cultural programs along with stories from streets, parishes, and local communities into several official live streams for distribution to Catholic media worldwide.
Media accreditation for the event will open separately, provisionally around May 2027, following procedures used at previous World Youth Days.
We are inviting you to help us build a network, Fr. Lee told delegates, describing SIGNIS members as a potential network of interpreters, collaborators, and trusted local voices.
Not every young person will be able to come to Seoul in 2027. But with you, World Youth Day Seoul 2027 can be present in local communities throughout the world, he concluded.
More information on World Youth Day Seoul 2027 is available at wydseoul.org.

world.title: SECAM: Recommends Establishment of Episcopal Commission for Catholic Education
world.desc:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
At the close of a two-day continental conference on Catholic education in Africa by the Symposium of Episcopal Conferences of Africa and Madagascar (SECAM), the participants recommended the establishment of a dedicated Episcopal Commission for Catholic Education, tasked with giving the continent's Catholic schools, universities, and formation institutions a coordinated structure for the years ahead.
Those who developed the Addis Ababa Declaration on Catholic Education, which was adopted on Friday, August 7, comprised the Presidents of the Episcopal Conferences, Bishops, Catholic educators, leaders of Catholic universities and schools, members of Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life, clergy, lay faithful, young people, and partners in Catholic education from across Africa and Madagascar.
According to the declaration, the proposed commission is expected to develop a SECAM Continental Framework for Catholic Education, establish mechanisms for collaboration, monitoring, evaluation, and reporting, encourage each Episcopal Conference to prepare national implementation plans, and convene periodic continental meetings to review progress, share best practices, and renew commitments.
Thus, it is designed to turn the declaration's broad commitments into a standing, continent-wide structure.
The declaration further insisted on shared responsibility. Citing the Final Document of the Synod on Synodality, the document frames the formation of the whole person as a task that requires synergy and co-responsible collaboration among all stakeholders in Catholic education and not just the work of the Church alone.
The declaration therefore calls on Episcopal Conferences to make Catholic education a pastoral priority by establishing functional national structures; on governments to recognize and support the contribution of Catholic institutions to national development; on Catholic universities and schools to strengthen quality assurance and governance; on religious congregations to continue investing in educational ministry; on parents to partner actively in their children's education and faith formation; and on development partners, the African Union, and other international bodies to collaborate in strengthening Catholic education throughout Africa and Madagascar.
In their message, the continental conference outlined commitments to strengthening ties among Catholic schools, universities, seminaries, religious congregations, and Episcopal Conferences across the continent, and promoting the sharing of gifts, resources, and experience between institutions and countries.
Organizers say the envisioned Episcopal Commission would serve as the practical vehicle for sustaining the collaboration, monitoring how well the different actors are working together and reporting back on shared progress.
Referencing the Gospel, Church teachings, the Global Compact on Education, the Kampala Document, and Africa's cultural heritage, the declaration reaffirms Catholic education as an essential ministry of the Church, a privileged instrument of evangelization, and a powerful force for character formation and integral human development.
The participants further acknowledged the historic contributions of Catholic schools and also recognized the growing challenges on the continent, including poverty, conflict, forced migration, unemployment, inequality, digital transformation, climate change, and declining moral values, alongside emerging opportunities in technology, research, innovation, and artificial intelligence.

world.title: MALAWI: Company Gives Smile to Life of CUNIMA Needy Students
world.desc:
By Luke Bisani
Smile Life Insurance Company has stepped up its support for higher education with a K5 million (3,000/= USD) donation to the Catholic University of Malawi (CUNIMA) Endowment Fund, aimed at helping needy and deserving students access university education.
Presenting the cheque at a ceremony held at the University, Smile Life Chief Executive Officer Ms. Beatrice Mangwana said the company recognizes education as a critical investment in developing the human capital needed to drive the country’s socio-economic development.
Ms. Mangwana said Smile Life was committed to supporting initiatives that create opportunities for young people to acquire quality education and contribute meaningfully to society.
She also commended CUNIMA for its holistic approach to education, saying the University’s graduates are equipped with knowledge and values that enable them to make a positive contribution to their communities and the nation.
Ms. Mangwana further described the 15-year relationship between Smile Life and CUNIMA as a strong partnership that demonstrates the value of collaboration between the private sector and higher education institutions.
Receiving the donation, CUNIMA Vice Chancellor Professor Francis Moto expressed gratitude to Smile Life for responding to the University’s call for support towards the Endowment Fund.
Professor Moto said the University has set an ambitious K1 billion fundraising target for the Endowment Fund, which is expected to enable CUNIMA to support 100 needy students every academic year.
“This contribution from Smile Life is a significant step towards achieving our goal of ensuring that deserving students are not denied access to higher education because of financial challenges,” said Professor Moto.
He disclosed that CUNIMA will hold a golf tournament in October this year as part of its fundraising drive and appealed to companies, organizations, alumni and well-wishers to support the initiative.
The Vice Chancellor said partnerships with the corporate sector are essential to ensuring the sustainability of the Endowment Fund and expanding opportunities for students from financially disadvantaged backgrounds.
CUNIMA launched the CHENS (Championing Higher Education for Needy Students) Endowment Fund last year as a long-term initiative to mobilise resources for students who demonstrate academic potential but face financial barriers to completing their university education.
With a target of K1 billion, the Endowment Fund represents one of CUNIMA’s major efforts to promote inclusive access to higher education, while the planned October golf tournament is expected to provide another platform for the corporate sector and other stakeholders to contribute to the initiative.
The University has since called on more partners to join Smile Life in supporting the Endowment Fund and helping more deserving students realise their academic aspirations.
